title: One authoring mistake reports up to five diagnostics: false follow-ons after a refused expression (14 of 60 probes)
body:
## Summary

One authoring mistake often reports several diagnostics, and only the first is true. After the verifier refuses an expression it keeps checking with a made-up type (usually `i64`) or with a name it never bound, so later checks fail against something the author did not write. For an agent each false line is tokens read and, at worst, a wrong edit.

I measured it instead of collecting anecdotes: **60 single-file programs, each with exactly one mistake** of the kind an author brings from another language. **14 of the 60 report more than one diagnostic**; the worst, one misspelled record name, reports five.

#49 item 8 fixed one instance of this class (`"a" < "b"` gave `SPX-T250` plus a false `SPX-T208`). These are the rest that I could find.

Baseline: `wavect/v0-10-0` at `a935c1b1ba46`, `semaprax check <file>`, debug build, Linux x86_64 (Docker, `rust:1` = rustc 1.99.0). Counts are local observations on that one build. No token or cost figure is claimed.

## The 14 cases

Every snippet is the body of `fn main() -> i64` (or the named helper) in an otherwise valid module with `@id`s.

| # | One mistake | Reported today |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `fn f(a: string, b: string) -> string { a + b }` | `SPX-T250`, `SPX-T103`, `SPX-O104` |
| 2 | `let s = "a" + "b"; string_len(s)` | `SPX-T250`, `SPX-T205` |
| 3 | `string_len("a" + "b")` | `SPX-T250`, `SPX-T205` |
| 4 | `if "a" + "b" == "ab" { 7 } else { 8 }` | `SPX-T250`, `SPX-T207` |
| 5 | `fn f(a: string) -> string { a * 3 }` | `SPX-T250`, `SPX-T103`, `SPX-O104` |
| 6 | `requires a + a == "xx"` (`a: string`) | `SPX-T250`, `SPX-T207` |
| 7 | `fn f() -> string { 1 }` | `SPX-T103`, `SPX-O104` |
| 8 | `let b = -true; if b { 1 } else { 0 }` | `SPX-T206`, `SPX-T210` |
| 9 | `let x: bool = 1; if x { 1 } else { 0 }` | `SPX-T232`, `SPX-T210` |
| 10 | `let x = abs(-3); x + 1` | `SPX-T203`, `SPX-T202` |
| 11 | `let p = Pont { x: 1, y: 2 }; p.x + 1` (no `Pont`) | `SPX-T001`, `SPX-T215`, `SPX-T212`, `SPX-T212`, `SPX-T202` |
| 12 | `fn f(a: int) -> i64 { a + 1 }` | `SPX-T001`, `SPX-T208` |
| 13 | `fn f(a: i64) -> int { a + 1 }` | `SPX-T001`, `SPX-T103` |
| 14 | `match s { Shape::Dot {} => 0, Shape::Square { w: w } => w, }` (case is `Box`) | `SPX-M103`, `SPX-T202`, `SPX-M101` |

Example, case 1 in full:

```
error[SPX-T250]: operator `+` does not support string operands at s01.spx:8:5
  help: join strings with `string_concat(a, b)`, which consumes both; …
error[SPX-T103]: function `f` returns i64, but its signature declares string at s01.spx:5:1
error[SPX-O104]: function `f` cannot return a value resource as owned at s01.spx:5:1
  help: return an owned resource or declare a future lifetime-bound view
```

The first line is exactly right and carries the fix. The function does not return `i64`, and there is no ownership problem.

The other 46 probes report exactly one diagnostic, including every unknown-function and unknown-value case used directly (`string_len(to_upper("a"))`, `if flag { … }`), so the verifier already has a working "unknown type" value (`None`); these 14 are the paths that do not use it.

## Root causes

| | Cause | Where | Cases |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | Arithmetic over a string still yields `i64` after `SPX-T250` | `src/source_verify/iterative/operators.rs` (`frame_resume_binary_right`), mirrored in `oracle.rs` | 1-6 |
| B | A refused unary operand still yields `i64`/`bool` after `SPX-T206` | `operators.rs` (`frame_resume_unary`), `oracle.rs` | 8 |
| C | A `let` whose initializer has no type binds nothing, so every later read reports `SPX-T202` for a name the source declares | `iterative/blocks.rs` (`Statement::Let`), name lookup in `iterative/enter.rs` / `oracle.rs` | 10, and the tail of 2, 8, 11 once A/B/G return no type |
| D | `SPX-O104` is judged on a body whose type `SPX-T103` just refused | `src/source_verify/declaration/functions.rs` | 7 (and 1, 5) |
| E | After `SPX-T232` the binding keeps the value's type, not the declared one | `iterative/blocks.rs` | 9 |
| F | A signature with an unknown type still has its body checked against it | declaration checks vs. body check | 12, 13 |
| G | An unknown record type also reports `SPX-T215` and one `SPX-T212` per field | `iterative/enter.rs`, `iterative/records.rs`, `oracle.rs` | 11 |
| H | An unknown match case binds none of its pattern names, and exhaustiveness is still judged | `iterative/matching.rs` / `match_arms.rs` | 14 |

## Proposal

A PR follows for A, B, C, D, E and G, which takes the corpus from 14 cascading cases to 3. The rule it holds to: a later diagnostic is dropped only on a path where an error was already reported for the same expression or initializer, so a refused program stays refused and the first, true diagnostic is never the one removed. No new verifier state or frame layout.

Left out on purpose, for your call:

- **F** needs the declaration pass and the body pass to share which signature types were refused; that is a wider change than the rest.
- **H** is pinned today by `tests/language/variants_semantics.rs` (`patterns_and_arm_results_are_checked_independently` asserts `["SPX-M103", "SPX-T202", "SPX-M101"]`). If that list is intended, case 14 is not a defect and should come off this list; if it is incidental, the pattern's names could be bound with no type and exhaustiveness skipped for a match that already has a refused arm.

## Two smaller observations from the same run

- `SPX-T001` for `int` reads "unknown type `int`; declare it with `resource int;`" while its own `help` line gives the right fix ("the integer types are `i64` …"). The message and the help point in different directions for the scalar habit names `unknown_type_help` already recognises. *(Corrected: I first wrote that the fix was missing; it is in the help line, which I had filtered out of my listing.)*
- `SPX-T223` (`Option<usize>`: "accepts only direct `i64` or `bool` arguments") carries no `help` line.

## Verification

The PR adds the corpus as one table-driven module in the `language` harness that pins the exact ordered codes for every case, so a new follow-on fails there. The three cases it leaves are pinned at today's lists in a separately named test, so fixing one is a conscious edit.
display_title: One authoring mistake reports up to five diagnostics: false follow-ons after a refused expression (14 of 60 probes)
